market_context: United States; USDA/FDA egg safety and quality guidance
title: How to Tell if an Egg Is Bad: Reliable Signs and Tests That Aren't

seo.title: How to Tell if an Egg Is Bad: Reliable Tests
seo.meta_description: The float test shows age, not safety. Learn what odor, shell condition, whites, unusual colors and dates can—and cannot—tell you about an egg.
seo.search_intent: Food safety: distinguish egg freshness tests from evidence of spoilage or unsafe handling.

excerpt: A truly spoiled egg usually has an unmistakable unpleasant odor when cracked. A floating egg is simply older because its air cell has enlarged; USDA notes that it may still be perfectly safe to use.
content_html:
Egg advice often confuses freshness with safety. As eggs age, the white becomes thinner and the air cell enlarges. Those changes affect quality, but they do not automatically mean the egg is spoiled—and they cannot tell you whether Salmonella is present.

The clearest spoilage sign: a bad odor after cracking

USDA says a spoiled egg will have an unpleasant odor when the shell is opened, whether raw or cooked. If you are uncertain, crack the egg into a separate bowl before adding it to other ingredients.

The float test measures age, not safety

Eggshells are porous. Over time, moisture and gases escape and the internal air cell gets larger. Eventually the egg becomes buoyant enough to float. USDA specifically states that a floating egg is of poorer quality but may be perfectly safe to use.

Water test resultWhat it suggestsWhat it cannot prove
Lies flat on bottomRelatively small air cellAbsence of pathogens
Tilts or stands more uprightOlder eggUnsafe egg
FloatsLarge air cell, lower freshnessSpoilage by itself

Shell condition matters

FDA recommends buying eggs with clean, uncracked shells. Cracks provide a route for bacteria to enter. If an egg has been cracked for an unknown amount of time, do not treat an intact-looking interior as reassurance.

Does a runny white mean an egg is bad?

No. Egg whites naturally thin as eggs age. USDA notes that cloudy albumen is associated with very fresh eggs, while a clearer white indicates aging. That is a quality change, not a safety verdict.

Unusual colors that deserve attention

Pink or iridescent egg white can indicate spoilage associated with Pseudomonas and should be discarded. A small blood spot, by contrast, results from a tiny blood vessel rupturing during ovulation and does not make the egg unsafe.

Yolk color mainly reflects the hen's diet and cannot tell you whether the egg is safe.

What about a green ring around a cooked yolk?

It is generally a cooking effect caused by sulfur and iron compounds, often after overcooking or slow cooling. USDA considers the green color safe to eat.

Dates and refrigeration

FDA recommends storing eggs promptly at 40°F (4°C) or below in their original carton and using them within about three weeks for best quality. FoodSafety.gov gives a broader 3–5 week refrigerator range for raw shell eggs. Dates and storage guidance are more useful than a float test when assessing how an egg has been handled.

Why a normal smell still cannot certify safety

Pathogenic bacteria do not need to make an egg smell rotten. That is why food-safety advice for raw or undercooked egg dishes focuses on pasteurized eggs, refrigeration and proper cooking rather than sensory inspection alone.

Tests that are not safety tests

  • Floating in water.
  • Shaking an egg and listening for movement.
  • Judging yolk color.
  • Looking only at how thick the white is.
  • Tasting raw egg to check it.

A practical check at home

  1. Check the carton date and storage history.
  2. Do not use eggs with problematic cracks or leakage.
  3. Crack questionable eggs one at a time into a separate bowl.
  4. Discard any egg with an unmistakable off odor or abnormal pink/iridescent white.
  5. Use pasteurized egg products for recipes that remain raw when appropriate.

Frequently asked questions

Should you throw away an egg that floats?

Not automatically. Floating means the air cell is large and the egg is older. USDA says it may still be safe.

Does a watery egg white mean spoilage?

No. Whites become thinner with age.

Are blood spots dangerous?

No. A small blood spot does not indicate an unsafe egg.

faq.question: Does a floating egg mean it is bad?
faq.answer: No. A floating egg is older because its air cell has enlarged; USDA says it may still be perfectly safe.

faq.question: What is the clearest sign of a spoiled egg?
faq.answer: A strong unpleasant odor after cracking is a clear reason to discard it.

faq.question: Does a watery white mean the egg is spoiled?
faq.answer: Not by itself. Egg whites naturally become thinner as eggs age.
